title: Routine maintenance visit and checklists
audience: Aquarium maintenance technicians who carry out recurring visits to client freshwater and marine tanks
learningOutcomes: Run a routine visit in a fixed order that covers the livestock, equipment, testing, water change, cleaning, filters and records
Use a checklist that sets out daily, weekly, monthly and longer tasks, and separates the owner's tasks from the contractor's
Carry out a staged partial water change that keeps the animals safe and keeps the bacteria in the filter
Reduce repeat work by sequencing tasks and recording only the exceptions
referencesAtStart: No official source is relied on in this lesson.

instruction.heading: A fixed order saves time
instruction.body: A routine visit goes faster and misses less when it follows the same order every time. A good order is: check safety and the work order, observe the livestock and the equipment, test the water, make the planned water change, clean the glass and décor, care for the filter, check the equipment and the lights, and then complete the records. Testing comes before the water change, because the results may change what the change should be. Observing the livestock before the work starts gives a baseline to compare with afterwards.

instruction.heading: Daily, weekly, monthly and longer tasks
instruction.body: Most daily tasks belong to the owner: feeding to the plan, a glance at the equipment and the livestock, and a check of the water level. The contractor's visit covers the tasks that need skill or access. Weekly tasks usually include the planned partial water change, glass and décor cleaning, a check of any top-off reservoir, and the planned tests. Monthly tasks include rinsing filter media in tank water, checking the lighting timer, and checking the expiry dates on test kits. Longer tasks include cleaning pumps and powerheads, calibrating probes, replacing bulbs at the manufacturer's interval, and checking heaters for age and condition. The intervals in the sources differ from one another and are examples only.

instruction.heading: The staged partial water change
instruction.body: A partial change removes waste from the bottom and replaces part of the water in small volumes. The method in the sources is to change part of the water, not all of it. Loosen the debris, siphon it from the gravel and the bottom, and refill slowly with treated water. Prepare the new water before you start, conditioned as the label directs and close to the tank's temperature. For a marine tank, match the salinity as well. Do not return siphoned water to the tank. When the siphon is finished, close the line so that the water in the hose does not run back into the tank. Keep the animals safe while you work. Where the plan allows, move them to a container of tank water with an air supply, and do not hold them out of water for long. Before you open a filter, check it for trapped fish, and never run a filter that has been opened and left dry.

instruction.heading: Glass, lights and décor
instruction.body: Clean the glass with a scraper or pad made for aquarium use, moving slowly so that the animals are not disturbed. Use only aquarium-approved supplies or clean water. Household cleaners are never used on glass, décor or equipment. Keep buckets for tank water only, because a bucket contaminated with cleaning residue can harm the animals. Before you remove a light from the tank or clean it, unplug it. Keep the light period to the plan, and set a timer if the owner forgets to switch the light off. Remove algae from décor and plastic plants by rinsing them in clean water, and replace any item that cannot be cleaned without damage. For live plants, remove dead leaves and keep the planting as the plan says.

instruction.heading: Filter care
instruction.body: Rinse biological media in tank water that was removed during the change, never in tap water, so that the bacteria survive. Clean mechanical media, such as sponge or floss, in the same way. If you replace floss, replace only part of it, and leave some of the original in the filter, because the old material keeps the bacteria the tank needs. Replace chemical media, such as activated carbon, only as the plan directs. Doing too much at once can strip the bacteria, so change one part at a time, and check the flow before you leave.

instruction.heading: The equipment check
instruction.body: Check the heater setting against the separate thermometer, the pump's flow and noise, the air line and air stone, the top-off device if one is fitted, the lighting timer, and every cord and outlet. Look for leaks at the tank seals and at the equipment joints. Any damaged item is taken out of service and referred (see the electrical safety lesson).

instruction.heading: Records and checklists
instruction.body: Use one checklist for each visit, with the same headings every time, and record only the exceptions in detail. A completed checklist shows that each task was done, or deliberately skipped with a reason. Record the time on site, each test result, the volume of any water change, the equipment checked, anything changed, and any observation about the animals. Save the record to the client's file on the day of the visit.

instruction.heading: What is outside a routine visit
instruction.body: A routine visit does not include adding medicines, treating animals, buying or moving animals, releasing water or animals, electrical or plumbing repair, or structural work. Record anything the owner asks for that is outside the visit, and refer it.

procedure: Confirm the work order, the tank's system type and the owner's plan, then complete the site safety check.
Observe the livestock, and record any sign of stress or disease with the time and the conditions.
Check the equipment from the outside: the heater, the pump, the filter flow, the air line, the timer and the cords.
Test the water at the planned point, and record each result before any change is made.
Make the planned partial water change in stages, using conditioned water at a close temperature, and keep the animals safe.
Clean the glass, lights and décor with aquarium-approved supplies, and rinse filter media in tank water.
Check the work against the checklist, and mark each task as done, skipped or referred, with the reason.
Record the visit, the results and any exceptions, and tell the owner about any referral.

workedExamples.situation: A routine visit is due. The owner asks you to skip the test because the tank looks clear, and to change half the water to save time.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do the test. A clear tank can still have rising ammonia or nitrate, and the results decide what the change should be. Keep the change to the planned volume. Refuse a half-tank change that the plan does not cover, explain why, and record the request and the decision. If the test shows a problem, follow the plan and refer any matter the plan does not cover.

workedExamples.situation: The filter media is clogged, and the client asks you to replace all of it and rinse the old media under the tap.
workedExamples.reasoning: Isolate the pump before you open anything. Rinse the biological media in tank water, not tap water, and replace only the part the plan directs. Keep some original media in place. Check the flow before you leave, and note the change on the record. Replacing all the media at once is a plan decision, and it is recorded as one.

equipmentAndPpe: Routine visit checklist for this system type
Test kit or meter, in date, and a sampling container for the tank
Siphon, bucket and scraper dedicated to this tank
Water conditioner, and conditioned new water prepared before the change

commonErrors.error: Testing after the water change, so that the result no longer shows the tank's state.
commonErrors.prevention: Test first, then decide the change.

commonErrors.error: Carrying out unplanned work on every visit.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the checklist to do what the plan requires, and record any skipped task with the reason.

commonErrors.error: Rinsing biological media in tap water.
commonErrors.prevention: Rinse media in tank water removed during the change.

commonErrors.error: Returning siphoned water to the tank.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove the siphoned water from the tank as the plan directs. Do not return it.

commonErrors.error: Leaving the light on all day.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the timer and the light period set by the plan.

commonErrors.error: Using household cleaners on the glass or equipment.
commonErrors.prevention: Use aquarium-approved supplies or clean water only.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Heavy tanks, cabinets and bags of substrate need a safe lift method. Get help for any lift that one person cannot manage safely.
Isolate electrical equipment before any work near a heater, pump, light or controller, as the electrical safety lesson describes.
Keep client records private, and share them only with the owner or a person the owner has authorised.

A routine visit does not grant any authority to treat or move animals, or to carry out electrical or plumbing work. Those tasks belong to the owner, a qualified person or a licensed person. This lesson grants no licence.

qualityStandard: Each visit follows the checklist, and each task is recorded as done, skipped or referred with a reason
Tests are completed and recorded before the water change is made
The water change is limited to the planned volume and uses conditioned water at a close temperature
Exceptions and referrals are recorded, and reported to the owner on the day
documentationEvidence: Completed checklist with done, skipped or referred status
Test results with time, temperature and tester
Water change record with volume and conditioning
Equipment check record, and any item taken out of service
Referral note for anything outside the visit
summary: Run each visit in the same order, and test before any water change.
Use the checklist to separate the owner's daily tasks from the contractor's, and mark every task as done, skipped or referred.
Change water in stages with conditioned water, keep the animals safe, and never return siphoned water to the tank.
Record exceptions and referrals, and refuse work outside the visit.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which order is best for a routine visit?
options: Water change, then test, then observe the livestock and the equipment in the tank
Observe the livestock and equipment, test, make the planned change, then record
Clean the glass first, then test the water, then observe the livestock
Replace the filter media before anything else, since it is the first thing to check

knowledgeChecks.question: How should biological filter media be rinsed during a visit?
options: Under hot tap water, which removes the dirt and the bacteria
With household detergent, which clears the media quickly
Not at all, because it never needs cleaning or rinsing
In tank water removed during the change, not tap water

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks for a larger water change than the plan sets, because the water looks cloudy. What should you do?
options: Do the larger change, because the client asked and the plan allows the owner to decide
Change the water with untreated tap water to save time, since the cloudy water needs replacing
Test first, record the result, follow the plan, and refer any request the plan does not cover
Add a product to clear the water quickly, so the client is happy with the tank at the next visit

knowledgeChecks.question: Where do the records come in the order of a routine visit?
options: At the start, before any check
